model_annotation: This figure presents pre-edit evaluation results for large language models (LLMs) on long-tail biomedical knowledge, as measured by accuracy (%) across different co-occurrence number groups from the CiKT dataset. The line plot on the left displays four methods: Base (blue solid line with circle markers), FT (green solid line with triangle markers), MEMIT (purple dashed line with square markers), and ROME (red dashed line with diamond markers). The x-axis represents co-occurrence number groups — <10¹, [10¹, 10²), [10², 10³), and ≥10³ — plotted on a categorical scale. The y-axis shows accuracy percentage, ranging from 55% to 65%, with major ticks at 55, 60, and 65. All lines show a general upward trend as co-occurrence numbers increase, indicating improved performance on more frequent (popular) knowledge. For instance, Base starts at ~57% for <10¹ and rises to ~63% for ≥10³; FT begins at ~58% and reaches ~64%; MEMIT starts at ~56% and ends at ~61%; and ROME begins at ~55% and climbs to ~60%. The table on the right provides detailed numerical results for five models — ROME, MEMIT, MEND, IKE, and FT — across the same four co-occurrence groups, reporting Edit, Reliability†, Gen.†, and Locality† scores. Best performance per group is bolded, second-best is underlined, and “†” indicates higher values reflect better performance, with “Gen.” standing for Generalisation. The accompanying text explains that LLMs struggle to capture long-tail biomedical knowledge during pre-training, with performance declining as co-occurrence numbers decrease, highlighting a significant gap between popular and long-tail knowledge handling.
